newsitem.title: UK: Japan expects chocolate boom to continue.
newsitem.headline: Japan expects chocolate boom to continue.

text.p: Sumo wrestlers may prefer rice, but Japan's new-found taste for chocolate is set to grow as more research points to its health benefits.

Akira Sasai, president of Japan's Chocolate and Cocoa Association, said on Monday manufacturers were hoping to revive a surge in demand which saw chocolate bar sales jump by 30 percent in the first nine months of 1996.

"There is room for increase if we campaign strongly. We are hoping that all age groups will start to eat chocolate," said Sasai, who is also the president of chocolate manufacturer Meiji Seika Kaisha.

He was talking to reporters following a presentation to the Council session of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) which, together with the Common Fund for Commodities, funded a project since 1993 to promote cocoa and chocolate demand in Japan.
Chocolate's image in Japan has improved dramatically since last year when consumers emptied supermarket shelves in response to television shows promoting its health aspects.
Food scientists from Japan and abroad were gathered to research into cocoa and chocolate, and their findings were presented to the media in two international symposiums held in 1995 and 1996.
It was found that, unlike the common view that cocoa is fattening, it contains stearic acid which lowers cholesterol levels and reduces neutral fats.
Cocoa also inhibited dental caries, stress and even cancer and arteriosclerosis, scientists concluded.
Substances in cocoa were also effective as anti-gastric ulcer drugs.
"People began to realise that if cocoa is good for you, chocolate must be too," said Sasai.
Demand has grown significantly after the campaigns which targeted schools, media and nutrition organisations.
But chocolate was still regarded as "children's candy" in Japan and most adults continued to shun it, Sasai said.
Out of a total confectionery production worth $34 billion, chocolate accounts for only about $4 billion, with Japanese confections and rice being the main rivals.
Consumption is still only half that in Europe, Sasai said.

However in the nine-month period between January and September 1996 total ground cocoa beans, mainly imported, increased to 36,000 tonnes from 30,000 in the year ago period. Production of sugared cocoa powder reached 365 percent of the previous year, Sasai said.
He added that it could take five more years for the Japanese to eat as much chocolate as the Europeans.
